analysis.one_liner: Protects about nine million acres of Utah red rock canyon country as wilderness, off-limits to new mining and drilling.
analysis.headline: A bill to protect roughly nine million acres of Utah canyon country as wilderness drew 168 House cosponsors but never got a committee vote and died when Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added roughly nine million acres of federal land in ten Utah regions — the Great Basin, Zion, Grand Staircase-Escalante, Moab, the San Rafael Swell, and others — to the National Wilderness Preservation System. Once designated, the land could not be leased for oil, gas, or geothermal development, staked for mining claims, or sold off. Existing livestock grazing and valid rights would have continued, and Utah's school trust lands inside the boundaries would be swapped for federal land of equal value.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses or values Utah's federal public lands: hikers, hunters, anglers, float-boaters, and future generations, who would get about nine million acres permanently shielded from development. Because the land is federally owned, it belongs to all Americans, and the bill's own findings cite big game hunting, multi-day float trips, and wildlife habitat as values worth protecting.

how_it_helps.text: Designates land in ten regions of Utah — from the Great Basin and Zion to the San Rafael Swell and the Book Cliffs — as wilderness, making it part of the National Wilderness Preservation System.
Withdraws the designated land from mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, so it cannot be opened to extraction or disposed of under public land laws.

The bill's findings emphasize values ordinary people use directly: big game hunting in the Book Cliffs, multi-day float trips down the Green River, canoe trips on the White River, and habitat for bighorn sheep, elk, and mule deer.
It reserves federal water rights for the wilderness areas with a priority date of enactment, helping keep enough water in desert streams to sustain them.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and mining companies lose access to mineral leasing and mining claims on the roughly nine million acres; off-road vehicle users lose motorized access inside wilderness boundaries. Utah gives up potential development revenue on state school trust sections inside the areas, though the bill requires the federal government to swap federal land of approximately equal value for them.

drawbacks.text: The designation is permanent and total: the land is withdrawn from mining claims and mineral and geothermal leasing, which Utah officials and energy interests argued would cost jobs and state and local revenue in a state where the federal government already owns most of the land.

Wilderness must be managed under the Wilderness Act, which bars roads and motorized travel inside boundaries, so off-road vehicle users and anyone who relies on motorized access would lose routes they use today.

Utah's state school trust sections inside the boundaries would have to be exchanged for federal land rather than developed, so the state forgoes any development revenue those sections might have produced.

The map was drawn and championed by members from outside Utah rather than negotiated with the state's own delegation, and county officials and Utah's Republican members argued the acreage was inflated and preferred locally negotiated, county-by-county public lands deals instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are large and permanent, and the bill took real care to soften the costs: existing grazing continues, valid existing rights are honored, road corridors get setbacks, state school lands are exchanged at equal value, and state wildlife authority is untouched. The strongest honest objection is process and place — a map authored largely by out-of-state members locked in acreage Utah's own delegation never accepted, in a state where federal ownership already limits the local tax base. Weighed honestly, the land is used and valued by far more Americans than the extraction and motorized interests affected, but the missing negotiation is why even some public-lands advocates saw a compromise bill as the more durable path.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittee — it got a hearing in October 2009 but never a committee vote or a floor vote — and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on April 2, 2009 with more than 100 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On April 29, 2009 it was referred to the Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands, the step where most wilderness bills wait for a markup.
A subcommittee hearing was held on October 1, 2009, but no markup or vote on the bill was ever scheduled in the subcommittee or the full committee.

By the end of the Congress on January 3, 2011, the bill had 168 cosponsors — 161 of 253 House Democrats and 7 of 178 House Republicans — yet it never reached the House floor, and no Senate companion vote was in play.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and mining companies and off-road vehicle users are better off: the roughly nine million acres stayed open to mineral leasing, mining claims, and motorized use, and no one ever had to vote against the protection on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy companies and off-road vehicle users

for.name: Rep. Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited more than 100 original cosponsors.

for.name: Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance and other conservation groups
for.what_they_did: Long campaigned for the Red Rock wilderness designation and mobilized public support for the bill.

against.name: Rep. Nick Rahall
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill, which stayed parked in subcommittee from April 2009 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Rob Bishop and Utah House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Red Rock wilderness designation and pushed instead for locally negotiated, county-level public lands legislation.

against.name: Sens. Orrin Hatch and Robert Bennett
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Red Rock wilderness designation in the Senate, so the bill had no realistic Senate path even if it had cleared the House.

against.name: Oil, gas, and mining interests and off-road vehicle groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the designation, arguing it locked away energy and mineral development and closed motorized routes.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic: 161 of 253 House Democrats cosponsored versus just 7 of 178 House Republicans, and no vote of any kind was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill withdraws roughly nine million acres of Bureau of Land Management land from mining claims and from mineral and geothermal leasing, permanently closing it to energy development. What the industry loses is exactly what the public gains in protected canyon country.

industries.industry: Off-road vehicle recreation (users, manufacturers, and user groups)
industries.note: Wilderness must be managed under the Wilderness Act, which bars roads and motorized travel, so ORV routes inside the boundaries would close. Motorized access for a segment of visitors is traded for quiet, non-motorized access for the rest.

The bill expressly allows existing livestock grazing to continue indefinitely within the wilderness areas, locking in current permit holders' access. Ranchers keep their livelihood, though taxpayers continue to underwrite grazing on federal land at below-cost rates.

Guides, outfitters, and gateway-town businesses around Moab, Escalante, and Boulder depend on unspoiled scenery and access for hunting, floating, and canyoneering, all of which the designation protects in the bill's findings. Their commercial interest runs directly alongside the conservation purpose.
